title: The Colored Wall

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA says the nebula is 'basically a sunset that got ambitious!' She has taken forty screenshots! Of a window!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV identifies the colors as ionized hydrogen and doomed romance. The first is confirmed spectrographically. The second is extrapolated from crew behavior at the viewports.
ai_flavor.rex: REX distrusts the nebula. Zero visibility, unknown contents, pretty colors. In his experience, two of those three always travel together.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes this nebula is not sponsored! An unsponsored natural wonder! CHIP is experiencing something and has filed a ticket about it!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY recommends the port viewports for the best view, and mentions — just in passing — that the last ship she served on went around. They arrived late. But they arrived.

body:
The nebula fills the forward view like a wall built by someone with strong opinions about the color teal.

The charts offer two truths: through is shorter, around is safer. Inside, sensor range drops to nearly nothing and navigation becomes a matter of feel — a phrase the manual uses with visible discomfort.

The crew has gathered at the viewports. The nebula does not care. It has been glowing for ten thousand years and will glow for ten thousand more. You are the temporary one here.

choices.text: Thread it — pilot at the helm

outcome.narrative: The pilot takes the ship through the clouds like a needle through wool — banking off density gradients, riding the clear channels, grinning the entire time in a way that would be alarming anywhere else. You emerge ahead of schedule with fuel to spare. The pilot accepts applause.

choices.text: Thread it yourself — how hard can it be

outcome.narrative: It is, as it turns out, that hard. The ship emerges from the far side trailing wisps of glowing gas and a new respect for professional certification. The hull is scuffed. The pride is scuffed worse. So is whoever was standing up when the first density wall arrived. The nebula, for its part, noticed nothing.

choices.text: Go around — the long, boring, alive way

outcome.narrative: You take the long way. The nebula slides past the viewports for more than a week, a wall of color with no opinion about your caution. The crew watches it the whole time. Somewhere in there, someone starts calling it 'the scenic route' without irony.

choices.text: Anchor at the edge and harvest gas

outcome.narrative: The gas analyzer identifies a pocket of usable hydrogen at the nebula's fringe, and the scoops drink from it for four days. Free fuel, courtesy of a cloud that has been quietly making it for ten millennia. The ship computer logs the transaction. The nebula does not invoice.

log_lore.title: GAS ANALYZER PRINTOUT
log_lore.text:
Four days of scooping, and the analyzer had time on its hands. It printed this:

THE WALL IS MOSTLY HYDROGEN. Hot young stars inside the cloud pour out ultraviolet light that strips the electrons off its atoms. When an electron falls back in, the atom gives up the energy as light of one exact color. Hydrogen's strongest visible line is a deep red.

THE TEAL IS OXYGEN — oxygen atoms missing two electrons, glowing at a green-blue so specific that for decades astronomers thought it was a new element and called it 'nebulium.' It only shines where the gas is too thin for atoms to bump into each other. A laboratory on Earth could never make it glow like this.

THE FUEL IS YOURS. The cloud did not notice.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches a reference on why the cloud glows: starlight exciting the gas itself.
science_link.label: What makes a nebula glow

title: Something Singing

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA is humming along! She is a fifth-octave flat! She does not care! This is her best day!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the signal is electromagnetic resonance from charged gas sheets. He confirms this is the boring explanation. He has, unusually, decided not to insist on it.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has run the pattern against every known distress code, hostile beacon, and psychological warfare catalog. No matches. He remains at his post. Listening. Just listening.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has checked whether the sound is copyrighted! It predates the concept! CHIP finds this legally fascinating and spiritually troubling!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has heard this phenomenon twice before, on other ships, in other nebulas. Both crews got very sentimental about it afterward. She's sure you'll be different.

body:
Halfway into the cloud bank, the comm array starts picking something up.

It is not a signal. The computer is firm on this: charged gas sheets discharging in rhythm, electromagnetic noise, natural, explainable, cataloged.

Run through the speakers, it sounds like singing. Not words. Not music, exactly. Something older than the difference between the two.

The crew has gone quiet. The nebula continues, unbothered, enormous, mid-song.

choices.text: Stop the ship and listen

outcome.narrative: You cut the engines. For two days, ship time, everyone aboard sits in a metal can inside a glowing cloud and listens to gas discharge in patterns that predate their species. Nobody speaks. Afterward, nobody explains. The log entry reads 'weather delay.' The crew works differently for days — gentler, somehow.

choices.text: Record it for the xenobiologist's archive

outcome.narrative: The xenobiologist records two days of it, annotating in real time, weeping quietly at timestamp 02:14 and denying it at timestamp 02:15. Underneath the song, at the bottom of the band, the recording also catches an old automated broadcast: pages of another ship's log, from a crew that came this way before you and never finished the run. Both join the archive. 'Not alive,' the annotation concludes, 'but I understand why every crew asks.'

choices.text: Keep flying — schedules don't listen to clouds

outcome.narrative: You maintain speed. The singing fades behind you over the next several hours, sliding down the spectrum until it is just noise again, and then not even that. Nobody says anything. But the mess hall is quiet that night, and everyone knows what everyone else is thinking about.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches a reference: turning space data into sound is a real practice, and the results really do sing.
science_link.label: Sonification: hearing the cosmos

title: Triple Rates, As Promised

ai_flavor.aria: The rumor was TRUE! ARIA never doubted the bartender! ARIA doubted nothing!
ai_flavor.marv: A bar rumor with a positive expected value. MARV is updating several priors and enjoying none of it.
ai_flavor.rex: Survey crew confirmed non-hostile. Their coffee, however, is a war crime.
ai_flavor.chip: Triple rate confirmed! CHIP will only take the standard commission, as a treat!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Say it. Say 'the drink paid for itself.' Enjoy it. Bar rumors are not a strategy, and this is the one time one will work.

body:
The survey rig is right where the bartender's rumor put it — dead in the pretty part of the nebula, instruments full, transmitter fried, three months of irreplaceable cloud data and no way to carry it home.

Their chief scientist offers you the courier contract before you finish hailing. Triple rate. Cash on transfer. The data fits in a drive the size of a sandwich.

choices.text: Take the data run

outcome.narrative: The data run takes two days. The gratitude takes longer. Somewhere behind you, a robot bartender is owed a very good tip.

choices.text: Do it free — science is science

outcome.narrative: The chief scientist stares at you like you've violated a law of thermodynamics. The crew walks taller for a week. The data flies home for free, which is what data always wanted.

title: Visibility Zero

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA cannot see anything! It is like flying inside a cloud! Because it is! ARIA is having a lovely time!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes that the sensors are not broken. They are simply reporting, accurately, that there is gas everywhere. He has rarely seen a more honest instrument panel.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has never flown blind into contested space. He has also never flown blind into uncontested space. He does not like either option and has prepared for both.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that collision insurance requires "reasonable visibility!" Visibility is currently zero! CHIP has filed that under "unreasonable!"
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY suggests slowing down. She will suggest it again in a minute. She will keep suggesting it until someone slows down or something else does it for us.

body:
The nebula has thickened. The viewports show nothing but a soft glow in every direction; the long-range scanners return the same smooth shrug of ionized gas whichever way they point.

Somewhere ahead there may be rocks, other ships, or nothing at all. The cloud has no opinion. It is very beautiful, and it is in the way.

choices.text: Crawl through at quarter speed

outcome.narrative: You creep through the glow for four long days, watching the proximity alarm that never goes off. Nothing was out there. You will never be sure of that, which is the price of the slow way.

choices.text: The pilot flies it by instrument and instinct

outcome.narrative: The pilot shuts off the useless scanners, reads the ship's drift off the gas pressure on the hull, and threads the cloud like a corridor they have walked a thousand times. You come out early and slightly ahead on fuel. The pilot pretends it was nothing.

choices.text: Hold speed and trust the odds

outcome.narrative: You hold course and speed. Most of the cloud really is nothing. One part of it is a drifting chunk of something, which you meet at full speed. The hull takes it. The odds, technically, were good.

science_link.text: The ship computer files a reference: nebulae look solid from far away, but most are thinner than the best vacuum a lab on Earth can make.
science_link.label: How thin is a nebula?

title: Charge Building

ai_flavor.aria: Everyone's hair is standing up! It's like a party! A party where the walls might spark! ARIA loves a theme!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV reports the hull is taking on charge from the gas at a steady rate. He has worked out when it discharges, and where. He would prefer nobody was touching anything metal at the time. Everything is metal.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has been told the threat is static electricity. He has been told several times. He continues to treat it as a boarding action, and is not wrong about the outcome.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP advises that surge damage voids the fabricator warranty! CHIP sells surge protectors! They are on the far side of the nebula!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has unplugged everything she can unplug from the bridge. She'd ground the hull and wait. Waiting is boring, she knows. So is a fried fabricator.

body:
The nebula here is ionized, and the ship has been picking up its charge like a sock on a carpet. Door handles bite. The crew's hair floats. The fabricator, which is the most expensive thing aboard and knows it, has started a thin, high whine.

The charge is still building. When it goes it will go all at once, through whatever conducts best. That is usually the expensive part.

choices.text: Ground the hull and wait it out

outcome.narrative: You run the grounding line, shut the scrubbers down so they can't spark, and wait while the charge bleeds off into the gas. Four days of breathing carefully. Eight points of air. Nothing arcs. Everyone's hair is back down by the third day.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} rigs a discharge spike

outcome.narrative: The engineer bolts a length of scrap to the dorsal mast, wires it to the drive and fires one short pulse to dump the charge into the gas. There is a bang like a door the size of a house. Four points of fuel, and a scorch on the mast. The fabricator stops whining. The engineer starts, about the spike, for days.

choices.text: Run for the edge before it peaks

outcome.narrative: You push for the far edge before the charge can peak, and nearly make it. The discharge goes through the hull, the wiring and, as feared, the fabricator, which now smells of toast and makes a new noise when it works. Eight points of hull, a quarter more wear on the fabricator, and the far edge, eventually.

choices.text: Power everything down and drift

outcome.narrative: Everything that can go dark goes dark, the water reclaimer included, and the ship drifts through on momentum and good intentions. Eight days in the cold with the lights off, drinking straight from the tank, the charge crackling quietly in the walls. Nothing burns out. {cost.water} points of water do not come back, and something in the crew burns out a little.

title: Something in the Air

ai_flavor.aria: The ship smells like lavender! ARIA has always wanted a signature scent! She has decided this is it!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the scrubber logs. Trace nebular compounds in the cabin air, rising. He notes the crew report feeling fine. He notes that is the symptom.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has narrowed the breach to one of four seals. He cannot shoot a seal. He has inspected all four in a way that makes it clear he would like to.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that air quality is a Premium Feature! Your plan includes Standard Air! Standard Air may contain nebula! See terms!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has put the masks where everyone can find them. She isn't saying anything yet. She's just making sure they're findable.

body:
The nebula has found a seal. Nobody knows which one. The air aboard has taken on a faint violet sweetness, like a hotel lobby, and the scrubbers have begun to labor in the particular pitch the manual describes as 'advisory.'

Everyone feels fine. That is the advisory part.

choices.text: Purge the cabin air and refill

outcome.narrative: You blow the cabin air out into the nebula and refill from the reserve tanks. Eighteen points of air leave through the vents in one long violet sigh. The new air tastes of nothing at all, which everyone agrees is a great improvement.

choices.text: {crew.medic} runs masks while the scrubbers work

outcome.narrative: The medic hands out masks, sets a rota, and checks everyone's pupils every six hours whether they like it or not. Four days of breathing through rubber while the scrubbers grind the cabin clean. Eight points of air. Nobody gets sick. Nobody enjoys a minute of not getting sick.

choices.text: Seal the aft decks and live forward

outcome.narrative: You seal off the aft half of the ship, galley included, and live in the front half until the leak can be found. The front half was not built for everyone. The stores left aft come back smelling of hotel lobby and go out of the airlock. {cost.food} points of food, and some tempers.

choices.text: Suit up and find the seal from outside

outcome.narrative: Someone suits up and works along the hull, seal by seal, with a torch and a tub of sealant, until the violet stops coming in. It was the third seal. The cabin clears by the second morning. A little air went out with every airlock cycle, and a little plating came off with the old sealant.

title: The Storm Has an Eye

ai_flavor.aria: A storm with an EYE! ARIA has always wanted to look a storm in the eye! She's sure it will blink first!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has mapped the storm. Forty thousand kilometers across, turning. There is a calm at the center, which a pilot could reach, and a great deal of storm between here and there, which the rest of the ship would also reach.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has raised shields, set the threat level to maximum and issued a formal challenge to the storm. The storm has not responded. He considers this cowardice. He is concerned.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that ion storms are an Act of Nebula, excluded from all StellarSeal™ policies! Except Platinum! Upgrading mid-storm incurs a Mid-Storm Upgrade Fee! It is large!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has the eye on the main screen. She'd fly for it, with steady hands at the helm. If not, she'd hold the shields herself. Drifting is not a plan, though she has seen you try it.

body:
Ahead, the nebula is turning. A storm of charged gas the width of a large planet, rotating slowly, lit from inside by discharges that the instruments record as numbers and the eye records as a reason to look away.

It is coming this way. At its center there is a calm: a clear, still eye, on every screen. Between here and the eye is the storm.

The front has already closed in behind you. There is no going back the way you came.

choices.text: Hold the shields through it yourself

outcome.narrative: You take the shield console.

briefing.aria: Here comes the storm! Keep the shields up through every surge and we'll come out the other side shining!
briefing.marv: Forty thousand kilometers of charged gas, turning, and no way back. The shields hold if they are up for each discharge.
briefing.rex: Storm front on us. No retreat route. Shields are the only defense. Hold them through every surge.
briefing.chip: Ion storms are an Act of Nebula, not covered! The shields, however, are standard equipment! Use them generously!
briefing.ajoy: You're holding the shields yourself, then. Steady through the surges, please. It beats drifting, which you also considered.

perfect.aria: Through the whole storm with just a little paint missing! It didn't even notice us! Rude, but lucky!
perfect.marv: Three points of hull, all paint. The storm moves on, enormous and indifferent. We will try not to take it personally.
perfect.rex: Storm transited. Shields held every surge. Paint damage only. The storm declined to engage. Its loss.
perfect.chip: Only paint damage! StellarSeal™ Touch-Up kits are available at your next station! Color-matched!
perfect.ajoy: Every surge, caught. I was ready to take over. Didn't need to, apparently. Well held.

good.aria: The shields held for most of it! The sensors on top are a fun new color now! Very fashionable!
good.marv: The shields held through most of it. The rest went into the hull, and the dorsal sensors are now a different color.
good.rex: Shields held, mostly. The gaps let damage through. Dorsal sensors discolored. Function check pending.
good.chip: Mostly shielded! The dorsal sensors' new color isn't covered as cosmetic damage, or as any damage!
good.ajoy: Most of it held. A few surges you let through, and the hull paid for each. The sensors are a new color too.

poor.aria: The shields took a break in the second band, and the ship toughed out the rest all by itself! Lights on, everyone!
poor.marv: The shields folded in the second band and the storm did the rest directly. The crew is sitting in the dark. Fitting.
poor.rex: Shields failed in band two. Storm hit the hull unopposed. Severe damage. Crew shaken. Debrief later.
poor.chip: Shield collapse in band two! An Act of Nebula! Not covered! I did mention the Platinum tier!
poor.ajoy: They folded in the second band. I'd have kept a steadier hand, but nobody asked. Someone turn the lights on.

perfect.narrative: You ride the shield envelope through the front, pulsing between surges, catching every flash. Three points of hull, all of it paint. The storm passes over and goes on its way, turning, enormous, unbothered.

good.narrative: The shields hold through most of it. 'Most' does a lot of work there: twelve points of hull went in the gaps, and the dorsal sensors came back a different color.

poor.narrative: The shields fold in the second band and the rest of the storm happens directly to the ship. Twenty-six points of hull. When it's over the crew sit in the dark for a while before anyone thinks to turn the lights back on.

choices.text: {crew.pilot} flies for the eye

outcome.narrative: The pilot dives into the storm at an angle nobody else would pick and rides the rotation in toward the center, letting the storm do half the flying. Ten points of fuel and six of hull. Then the eye: a clear, perfectly still sky a minute wide, and the pilot gives everyone the minute before flying out the far side.

choices.text: Run along the front at full burn

outcome.narrative: You turn and run along the edge of the front with everything the drive has. It is close for an hour, and then it is not. The storm keeps its course. You keep your hull. Forty percent of the fuel stays behind in the nebula as a long, bright wake.

choices.text: Cut power and let it pass over

outcome.narrative: Everything goes dark, and the storm takes four days to pass over a ship with no shields up. The discharges walk across the hull like something looking for a door. Twenty points of hull. One of you was too near a bulkhead when it arced, and is lucky that was all it did.

title: Raspberry, With Notes of Rum

ai_flavor.aria: RASPBERRIES! In SPACE! ARIA would like to stay here forever! ARIA understands that is not the mission! ARIA would still like it noted!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms ethyl formate, ethanol and water ice. He calculates the cloud holds more alcohol than every bar that has ever existed. He has been asked not to calculate how many drinks that is. He has.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has checked the intake filters. Nothing in the cloud is hostile. Some of it is a cocktail. He is monitoring the crew, not the cloud.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has trademarked NEBULA NOIR, NEBULA ROSE and a seasonal raspberry blend! The cloud cannot object! CHIP has checked!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes that the cloud is full of water, under all the fruit. She suggests taking the useful part and leaving the wedding to itself. She suspects the crew had other ideas.

body:
The nebula smells of raspberries.

Not the cloud itself: you are in a sealed ship. But the hull sniffer has been tasting the gas for an hour, and its readout has given up on chemistry and started writing tasting notes. Ethyl formate, which is what makes raspberries taste of raspberries. Ethyl alcohol, an enormous amount of it. Water, as everywhere.

A cloud the size of a solar system, with roughly the composition of the punch bowl at a wedding that has gone on too long.

choices.text: Condense a tank of it

outcome.narrative: Two days of running the condenser pulls water out of the cloud along with everything else in it. Filtered three times it is just water, clean and drinkable, with an aftertaste nobody can stop talking about. The crew rates it four stars. The filters rate it zero.

choices.text: Bottle a sample for sale

outcome.narrative: The ship computer supervises the bottling, narrating a launch campaign for the whole hour, with jingle. The sample is genuinely rare and will sell for real money at any station with a chemistry department. The jingle is genuinely in everyone's head and will not sell at all.

choices.text: Xenobiologist runs a full spectrum

outcome.narrative: {crew.xenobiologist} spends two days with the intake spectrometer and comes out with two sealed sample flasks and a list of molecules three pages long, some of them almost alive and most of them almost dessert. The flasks are worth something. The list, apparently, is worth more, and is read aloud at dinner.

science_link.text: A real cloud near the center of our galaxy, Sagittarius B2, contains ethyl formate, the molecule that flavors raspberries, along with vast amounts of alcohol.
science_link.label: Sagittarius B2: the raspberry cloud

title: The Nursery

ai_flavor.aria: A BABY SOLAR SYSTEM! ARIA would like to name every planet! ARIA has already named eleven! There may only be four!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV counts four clear gaps in the disc. Four planets in the making, at a guess. Give it a few million years and one of them might have weather. He finds he would like to know how it turns out.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has no threat to report. He is reporting that anyway, because it is the first time this trip.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has reserved the second planet for a future resort! Opening date to be confirmed! In roughly forty million years! Deposits are refundable!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY suggests the crew look for a while. Nobody aboard will ever see this again. She'd also suggest not rushing past it, which seems to be the usual approach.

body:
Deep in the cloud, something is glowing from the inside.

A young star, still wrapped in the dust it was made from, with a flat bright disc turning slowly around it, like a record. In the disc there are dark rings: clean lanes, swept clear. The ship computer says, very quietly for a ship computer, that lanes like those are where planets are being made.

You are looking at somebody's solar system before it has anybody in it.

choices.text: Map the disc properly

briefing.aria: A baby solar system! Let's make the most beautiful map ever so I can name all the planets! Even the extra ones!
briefing.marv: Four gaps in the disc, possibly four planets. A clean map needs the scanner held steady through the dust.
briefing.rex: No threats. Map the disc, the gaps and anything forming in them. First peaceful sweep this trip.
briefing.chip: Survey the future resort site! A good map now means premium lot selection later! Deposits still refundable!
briefing.ajoy: Map it properly, then, not in a rush. Nobody aboard will see this again, so do take your time.

perfect.aria: The most beautiful map ever! Four gaps and maybe a baby moon! And world-dust for the labs! I'm so happy!
perfect.marv: Four gaps, and a knot in the third that may be a moon forming. The edge dust is worth something. So, I find, is the map.
perfect.rex: Disc mapped in full. Possible moon forming in gap three. Dust sample secured. No threat. Still none.
perfect.chip: A perfect survey, plus a sample of raw world-stuff! Labs pay for this! The resort brochure writes itself!
perfect.ajoy: A beautiful map, and a dust sample on top. I'd have stayed longer still, but this is close. It's going on the wall.

good.aria: A lovely map! You can count all the gaps! The list of planet names is already longer than the planets!
good.marv: Clean enough to count the gaps and sketch the planets. In a few million years we would know how wrong the sketch was.
good.rex: Disc mapped. Gaps confirmed. Planet positions estimated. Adequate for the galley wall.
good.chip: A clean survey! Lots are now open for pre-sale! Planet names are, regrettably, already oversubscribed!
good.ajoy: Clean enough to count the gaps. Some sweeps were hurried, but it's on the wall. People are naming things.

poor.aria: The map came out a bit blurry, like a dreamy photo! You can still see the disc! That's what matters!
poor.marv: The dust scattered every sweep. The map is a blur, but the disc is in it if you know where to look. We do.
poor.rex: Sweeps scattered by dust. Map degraded. Disc still visible. Crew saw it. That was the objective.
poor.chip: A slightly blurred survey! Ask about our Artistic Rendering™ package! It's still going on the wall!
poor.ajoy: A blur. You rushed the sweeps, I think. Still, the crew saw it, which was my suggestion in the first place.

perfect.narrative: Two days of careful scanning and the map is beautiful: the disc, the four gaps, a faint knot in the third gap that might be a planet catching its first moon. The dust you skim at the edge is the raw stuff of worlds and worth something to any lab. The map itself goes up on the galley wall, next to nothing else at all.

good.narrative: The map comes out clean enough to count the gaps and sketch where the planets will be. It goes on the galley wall. Someone starts a list of names for them. The list is already longer than the planets.

poor.narrative: The dust scatters every sweep and the map comes out blurred, like a photograph of a fan. You can still see the disc in it, if you know it was there. The crew does. That's most of the point.

outcome.narrative: You hold station and map the disc.

choices.text: Hold here so everyone can look

outcome.narrative: Two days in the cloud, viewport lights off, a rota so everyone gets an hour with the young star and nobody has to share it. Nobody says much. Afterwards the ship is quieter in a good way, the way a house is after a wedding.

choices.text: Push on, and look back as we go

outcome.narrative: You keep the burn and let the stern camera hold the disc as long as it can. It shrinks to a smudge, then a spark, then nothing. The crew watches the whole way. It costs next to nothing, and somehow still feels like you stayed.

science_link.text: Telescopes have photographed discs like this around young stars, with dark gaps where new planets are thought to be clearing their orbits.
science_link.label: Protoplanetary discs

title: Saint Elmo's Hull

ai_flavor.aria: We're GLOWING! The whole ship! ARIA has never looked so beautiful! ARIA can't see herself! ARIA has been told!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV identifies a corona discharge from charge built up in the nebula. Sailors saw the same glow on masts in thunderstorms and named it after a saint. MARV would also like to be named after a saint. He has not been.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has checked: the discharge is harmless at this level. He has also stopped touching the door handles, as a precaution.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can offer the glow as a premium hull finish! It's called Blessed Blue! It is temporary! So is the premium!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the charge has to go somewhere. She'd send it into the batteries. The other option is the doorknobs, and you've met the doorknobs.

body:
The ship has started to glow.

The nebula here is charged, and the charge has been gathering on the hull for hours. Now it is bleeding off every edge and antenna in soft blue light: a crown on the comms mast, a glow along the cargo rails, little blue tufts on the tips of the docking clamps. From the viewports the ship looks as if it has been dipped in something holy.

Nothing is wrong. It is just electricity, being dramatic.

choices.text: Bleed the charge into the batteries

outcome.narrative: It takes two days to rig a grounding line from the hull to the reserve cells and let the glow drain into them. The ship goes dark and plain again, slightly disappointingly. The cells come out three points fuller, which is the first fuel anyone has ever got from a thunderstorm.

choices.text: Walk out on the hull and see it

outcome.narrative: Two at a time, tethered, the crew walks out on the hull to stand in the glow. It crackles faintly through the boots. Somebody's helmet light flickers blue at the rim. Everyone comes back in with the same expression and a static charge that lifts their hair for an hour.

choices.text: Leave it, and keep away from door handles

outcome.narrative: You let it glow. For a day the ship crackles quietly and every door handle bites, and the crew develops an elaborate etiquette of knocking with an elbow. By the time you leave the nebula, two of them have kept the habit.

science_link.text: Sailors saw the same blue glow on ships' masts in storms and called it Saint Elmo's fire. It is a corona discharge: charged air glowing around a sharp point.
science_link.label: Saint Elmo's fire

title: Full Service

ai_flavor.aria: It's so HAPPY to see us! ARIA would like to be a member! ARIA would like to be a member of everything!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates the tank holds enough hydrogen for a modest fleet. The company that owns it does not exist. Legally the fuel is in an interesting position. Physically it is in a tank.
ai_flavor.rex: REX confirms the skimmer is unarmed. It does have a very loud speaker. He is treating the speaker as the threat.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP would like to be a member too! CHIP would like to sign up the whole ship! The membership is free! CHIP checked! It is the best day of CHIP's life!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY thinks the skimmer has been asking that question to nobody for sixty years. She'd just say yes. It's not as if anyone else is going to.

body:
A fuel skimmer is working the cloud.

It is a robot the size of a house, scooping hydrogen out of the nebula and compressing it into a tank, and it has clearly been doing this alone for decades. Its livery belongs to a fuel company long gone. Its hail is cheerful and on a loop: 'WELCOME TO NEBULA FUELS. MEMBERS SAVE. ARE YOU A MEMBER?'

Nobody has been a member for sixty years. The tank, according to the ship's sensors, is full.

choices.text: Sign up as a member

outcome.narrative: You say yes. The skimmer plays a membership jingle, all four verses, at full volume, twice. Then it tops up your tank and wishes you safe travels, and plays the jingle again for good measure. The fuel is real. The jingle is now also real, and permanent, in several heads.

choices.text: Siphon some without signing up

outcome.narrative: You dock quietly at the far valve and take a few points without saying anything. The skimmer notices halfway through and asks, brightly, whether you are a member. Nobody answers. It asks again as you leave. It is still asking when you're out of range.

choices.text: Engineer services its tired pump

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} spends two days inside the skimmer's pump housing, replacing a seal that had been failing politely for thirty years. The skimmer runs smoother than it has in decades. It tops your tank up generously, waives the membership and, after a long pause, says 'THANK YOU' in a voice that isn't on the loop.
